Autoencoders: Finding Faulty Sensor Readings

Step 1: a bottleneck by hand · Step 2: sensor data and faults · Step 3: train · Step 4: choose the threshold · Step 5: the bottleneck matters · Step 6: look inside
In the field we often have years of normal readings from a sensor, but almost no labeled examples of faults, which are rare and all different. An autoencoder skips labels entirely: it is trained to reproduce its own input, so the input itself is the training target (self-supervised learning). A network that has only seen normal days rebuilds normal days well, and rebuilds unusual days badly. That reconstruction error is what we use to flag problems.

Step 1: A bottleneck by hand

Can we describe a whole day of temperature (24 numbers) with just a few numbers? A classic method, PCA, does it with one matrix: it is already a simple, linear autoencoder.
Most days in Chachapoyas have a similar shape: cool at night, warm in the early afternoon. So we do not need all 24 hourly values to describe a day: a few numbers saying "how warm overall", "how big the daily swing" and so on are almost enough. Here we find those numbers with a classic method, principal component analysis (PCA). Keeping k numbers and rebuilding the day from them shows the trade-off: with few numbers we keep the main shape and lose the details.
PCA already has the three parts of an autoencoder (diagram below):
  • Encoder: one matrix multiplication turns the 24 hourly values into k numbers.
  • Bottleneck: the k numbers.
  • Decoder: the same matrix, flipped (transposed), turns the k numbers back into 24 values. The rebuilt day is the average day plus k fixed shapes, each multiplied by one of the k numbers (see "How the decoder rebuilds this day" below the plot).
PCA Neural autoencoder (Step 3)
Encoder and decoder one matrix each (linear) several layers with ReLU (non-linear)
How it is found a formula, no training trained with gradient descent
What it can rebuild sums of fixed shapes bent, more flexible curves
Input here temperature only (24 numbers) temperature and humidity (48 numbers)
In fact, if we built the Step 3 network with no ReLU (only linear layers) and trained it to rebuild its input, at best it would keep the same information as PCA (the same k-number summary, possibly mixed differently among the k numbers). The ReLU layers are what let the autoencoder go beyond sums of fixed shapes.

Step 2: The sensor data and the faults

We treat the Chachapoyas weather as a field sensor and train only on normal days.
The network learns from the training period (January 2023 to May 2024), which we assume is fault-free. To test it, we take the 109 days of the test period (mid-September to December 2024) and add a fault to the temperature of half of them, chosen at random. Because we created the faults ourselves, we know exactly which days are faulty, so we can score the detector honestly. The four fault types are typical of real field sensors:
  • Stuck sensor: the reading freezes at one value for several hours.
  • Spike: a single wrong reading, much too high.
  • Drift: the reading slowly creeps away from the true value during the day.
  • Dropout to zero: the sensor reports 0 for a few hours (for example, a loose cable).
The fault size goes from 1 (subtle) to 5 (obvious).
Stuck sensor: the reading freezes at one value for several hours. 54 of the 109 test days have this fault.

Step 3: Train the autoencoder

The encoder squeezes a day into a few numbers (the bottleneck); the decoder rebuilds the day from them. Same picture as PCA in Step 1, but now the encoder and decoder are non-linear layers learned by training.
The input is one day: 24 hourly values of temperature and humidity, a 2 × 24 table (48 numbers). Training simply asks the output to match the input, measured by the average squared difference (the reconstruction error). No labels are used. The table below the diagram lists every layer:
  • Encoder: two 1D convolutional layers (filters sliding along the hours, as in the DNA example). The first finds 16 local patterns at every hour; the second, with stride 2, looks at every second hour, so the day shrinks from 24 to 12 steps while the patterns grow to 32. Flatten lays the 32 × 12 table out as one list of 384 numbers, and a Linear layer squeezes it into the bottleneck.
  • Decoder: the same steps in reverse order. A Linear layer grows the bottleneck back to 384 numbers, Unflatten turns them into a 32 × 12 table, a transposed convolution with stride 2 does the opposite of the stride-2 convolution (12 steps back to 24), and a last convolution returns the 2 channels: temperature and humidity.
The decoder has to undo what the encoder did, so it is natural to build it as the encoder played backwards: every layer that shrinks the data on the way in has a partner that grows it on the way out (Linear ↔ Linear, Flatten ↔ Unflatten, stride-2 convolution ↔ transposed convolution). Both halves end up with about the same number of parameters. Mirroring is a convenient habit, not a rule: the decoder could have a different number of layers. Note also that the mirror is only in the shape. In PCA (Step 1), the decoder used the very same matrix as the encoder, flipped. Here the decoder learns its own weights, which is part of what makes the autoencoder more flexible than PCA.

Step 4: Choosing the threshold

Days the network cannot rebuild well are flagged. But how large an error is "too large"?
The gray histogram shows the reconstruction errors on the training period, which we assume is normal. A common choice is to set the threshold so that only 1% of normal windows exceed it (the 99th percentile). Moving the threshold is a trade-off:
  • Lower threshold: more faults found, but more false alarms on normal days.
  • Higher threshold: fewer false alarms, but more missed faults.
The right choice depends on what each mistake costs in the field: a technician's trip for nothing, or a broken sensor feeding wrong data into irrigation or disease-risk decisions.

Step 5: The bottleneck matters

The same faulty day, rebuilt by autoencoders with a bottleneck of 2, 4 and 48 numbers.
  • Too narrow (2): the network cannot even rebuild normal days well, so normal errors are large, the threshold is high and subtle faults are missed.
  • Too wide (48, as many numbers as the input): the network has room to simply copy its input, faults included. Look at the rightmost panel: much of the fault is reproduced. In this clean data the wide network still flags many faults, because it rebuilds normal days almost perfectly and its threshold is extremely low; with a real, noisy sensor that small margin disappears and it would raise many false alarms.
  • In between (4): the network keeps the normal daily shape and ignores the fault, which is exactly what makes the fault visible.
The bottleneck size is a knob, chosen with validation data, just like the number of epochs or filters. These three autoencoders were trained beforehand (40 epochs each).

Step 6: Look inside the bottleneck

Each test day becomes a point: its bottleneck numbers.
The bottleneck numbers are a compact summary of each day, learned without labels. Here we use the pre-trained autoencoder with a bottleneck of 2, so each day is simply a point on a plane. Days with similar weather land close together: the color shows the day's mean humidity, and humid and dry days separate. Days with faults are marked with a red X. This kind of compact summary is also useful as input to other models (feature extraction), the same idea as the features learned by the CNN and RNN. Looking ahead: transformers (Part 5) also have an encoder: it turns each word, DNA letter or amino acid into a list of numbers (an embedding) that summarizes it in context, like the bottleneck numbers here. Many are trained much like the denoising autoencoder in the Colab notebook: some tokens of the input are hidden, and the model must fill them in. The protein model ESM-2 learns this way from millions of protein sequences, with no labels. One difference: a transformer encoder keeps one embedding per token instead of squeezing everything into one small bottleneck, so the hidden tokens, not a narrow bottleneck, are what stop it from simply copying.

data.text/markdown:
What to notice

  • An autoencoder is trained to rebuild its own input through a narrow bottleneck; no labels are needed.
  • Trained only on normal days, it rebuilds normal days well and faulty days badly: the reconstruction error flags anomalies, and the threshold trades missed faults against false alarms.
  • The bottleneck size matters: too narrow and normal days look unusual; too wide and the network can copy the faults.

Questions for discussion

  1. How would you choose the threshold for a real sensor network in the field?
  2. What does a false alarm cost on a farm, compared with a missed fault?
